rw.headline: Evra Honors Genocide Victims Before Gorilla Naming Ceremony
rw.dek: Former footballer Patrice Evra visited the Kigali Genocide Memorial ahead of Rwanda's annual Kwita Izina gorilla naming event.
paragraphs: Former Manchester United player Patrice Evra paid tribute to victims of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi during a visit to the Kigali Genocide Memorial. Evra is in Rwanda to participate in the 21st edition of Kwita Izina, the country's annual gorilla naming ceremony, scheduled for September 4, 2026, in Kinigi. The memorial serves as a site for remembrance and education, preserving the memory of over one million people killed during the genocide.

Evra is among several international figures invited to this year's Kwita Izina, where he is expected to name one of 22 baby mountain gorillas. The ceremony in Musanze District is a prominent conservation event that draws global attention to Rwanda's efforts in protecting endangered mountain gorillas. His participation, due to his high profile, is anticipated to provide additional international spotlight on the event.

The Kwita Izina celebrations will be followed by a concert in Kigali featuring Afrobeats star Rema and Rwandan artist Kenny Sol. This event aims to celebrate the conclusion of the gorilla naming festivities through music. The combined activities, from remembrance to conservation and entertainment, highlight Rwanda's efforts in rebuilding and promoting its national story on an international stage.

rw.headline: Rwanda Deputy Governor Urges Action on AML Rules
rw.dek: Nick Barigye stated that anti-money laundering systems must demonstrate measurable results in disrupting financial crime, not just compliance.
paragraphs: Countries in Eastern and Southern Africa are being urged to move beyond simply meeting regulatory requirements for combating money laundering and instead focus on achieving tangible results against financial crime. This call came during the 2026 Annual Meetings of the Eastern and Southern Africa Anti-Money Laundering Group (ESAAMLG), attended by representatives from 22 member states and international bodies like the FATF, World Bank, and IMF.

Rwanda’s central bank Deputy Governor, Nick Barigye, emphasized that the true measure of anti-money laundering systems lies in their effectiveness at disrupting illicit financial flows, recovering criminal assets, and dismantling networks. He highlighted the increasing cross-jurisdictional nature of financial crime, stressing the critical need for enhanced international cooperation and faster exchange of financial intelligence to track and recover proceeds hidden through complex corporate structures.

The challenge is substantial across the region, with Rwanda's Financial Intelligence Centre reporting fraud, embezzlement, human trafficking, illegal foreign exchange, and tax evasion as frequent crimes between 2019 and 2024. Officials noted that identifying money movement is insufficient; authorities must also uncover beneficial ownership to link suspicious transactions to individuals. Delays in information exchange remain a major concern, allowing criminals to move assets, underscoring the need for closer collaboration among various national and international agencies.

st.headline: Vila Nova seeks unity for political stability in second term
st.dek: President Carlos Vila Nova called for greater union and responsibility, emphasizing the nation's need for political stability during his inauguration.
paragraphs: President Carlos Vila Nova, beginning his second term, urged greater unity and responsibility among São Tomé and Príncipe's citizens, stating that "São Tomé and Príncipe needs political stability." He declared that his second term marks a "new stage of greater union, greater responsibility, greater collective ambition" towards sustainable development. Vila Nova stressed that leaders must understand power is not a personal possession and that political differences should not become national animosities.

The President advocated for a culture of cooperation and dialogue between established powers, emphasizing interdependence within the separation of powers. "We need to build bridges where walls have often been built," he stated. Vila Nova believes in the strength of democracy through listening to differing viewpoints, asserting that strong nations are built on dialogue, respect, tolerance, and transforming differences into solutions, not artificial unanimities.

Vila Nova expressed gratitude for the trust placed in him by the São Tomé and Príncipe people for a second mandate, viewing it as a renewed responsibility to the nation and the world. He thanked supporters, political parties, and even those with different visions. Vice-President of the National Assembly, Arlindo Barbosa, also spoke, wishing the President health, wisdom, serenity, and strength for his five-year term.

st.headline: Tchiloli Theatre Actors Champion Justice in Sao Tomé
st.dek: Actors in elaborate costumes perform medieval European tragedies in open-air theatre that has remained popular for over 500 years.
paragraphs: Open-air Tchiloli theatre, a tradition introduced over five centuries ago by Portuguese colonists, continues to draw crowds in Sao Tomé. Actors don elaborate outfits, complete with beards, wigs, and hats, to perform medieval European tragedies on the island off Africa's west coast. The tradition's enduring popularity is attributed by performers and spectators alike to its consistent message of justice.

Marc Carvalho, a troop member for 35 years, believes the theatre's appeal lies in its unwavering advocacy for justice, stating, "Justice does not distinguish between rich and poor." This sentiment is echoed by spectator Maribel Borja, who noted that the plays convey a crucial message about fairness for all social classes and religions. The scripts, written in Old Portuguese, are drawn from legends of the Carolingian dynasty.

The performances are demanding, with actors spending hours on stage. However, Jardel Moniz Fernandez finds the work energizing and plans to involve his own children in the tradition. He intends to begin training his oldest son to play a character who delivers a letter, ensuring the continuation of his family's involvement in the Tchiloli theatre.

sn.headline: Senegal Restructures $5 Billion Debt, Triggers Default Countdown
sn.dek: The nation's debt, already struggling, saw an immediate drop in value as investors reacted to the restructuring plan with the IMF.
paragraphs: Senegal has initiated a $5 billion (2,830 billion CFA francs) bond restructuring, a move that signals the start of a countdown to potential default, according to Bloomberg. The government revealed a rescue plan with the International Monetary Fund on Tuesday, aimed at reorganizing these eurobonds. This development addresses a two-year question for emerging market investors: could Senegal avoid becoming the first African nation to default since Ethiopia in 2023?

The country's debt, already classified as distressed, experienced an immediate decline in market value following the announcement, suggesting some investors were caught off guard. While Dakar has not explicitly declared a default, countries utilizing the G20 Common Framework have historically halted debt repayments during negotiation periods. A critical test arrives on September 13, the due date for an interest payment on a eurobond.

The financial countdown is paralleled by a political one. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye dismissed Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko, who had strongly opposed restructuring, in May. Now Speaker of the National Assembly, Sonko reacted to the IMF deal on Facebook, calling for a "healthy debate on Senegal's commitments." The operation also tests how sovereign borrowers handle controversial yield-swap instruments, which the IMF has criticized.

sn.headline: Ethiopian student caught with 3 kg of khat in Dakar
sn.dek: Dakar police arrested a 35-year-old Ethiopian national with three kilograms of khat, a stimulant plant, following an investigation into a drug trafficking network.
paragraphs: Dakar's regional narcotics brigade (BRS) arrested a 35-year-old Ethiopian man on September 2, 2026, in the Médina district. The individual, who identified himself as a student living in Gueule-Tapée, was found in possession of three kilograms of khat. The arrest followed an investigation prompted by intelligence about a khat trafficking network operating between the Médina and Gueule-Tapée neighborhoods, allegedly led by a foreign national.

Investigators received operational intelligence indicating the existence of the drug network. Using information from an informant, police obtained the phone number of the suspected ringleader. After confirming the intelligence through a controlled delivery operation, officers set up surveillance in Gueule-Tapée near a canal, the designated meeting point. They observed an individual matching the suspect's description carrying a bag.

The suspect was apprehended, and a search of his bag revealed three kilograms of khat. A subsequent search of his residence yielded no further evidence. The man, identified as Y. M. Ismail, was taken to the BRS headquarters in Dakar, and the seized khat and mobile phones were secured for evidence. Khat, a plant chewed for its stimulant effects, is banned in many countries due to its addictive properties and potential health risks.

sn.headline: Senegal Health Minister Pushes Healthier Diets and Clearer Food Labels
sn.dek: Health Minister Dr. Ibrahima Sy advocates for collective action to combat non-communicable diseases through improved nutrition and food labeling.
paragraphs: Dakar's municipal council convened an workshop on Thursday, September 3, 2026, focusing on non-communicable diseases linked to diet and food product labeling. The event, part of the "Dakar PHC – Partnership for Healthy Cities" project, aims to involve local elected officials in promoting healthier eating habits. The initiative seeks to empower consumers to better understand food composition, specifically salt, sugar, and fat content.

Minister of Health Dr. Ibrahima Sy emphasized the need for a united front against the rise of non-communicable diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular, and kidney ailments. He called for coordinated efforts between the state, local authorities, and partners to strengthen prevention strategies. Clearer labeling is seen as a crucial tool for enabling informed consumer choices and fostering healthier food environments.

The initiative places particular emphasis on protecting children and vulnerable populations, who are more susceptible to the adverse effects of unbalanced diets. Health authorities view prevention as a key strategy for ultimately reducing the burden of non-communicable diseases on both the population and the healthcare system. This approach underscores the link between dietary choices and public health outcomes.

sn.headline: Three TikTokers jailed pending public indecency trial
sn.dek: Rox, Jessica, and Narou will spend their first night in detention after being placed under arrest warrant by the Pikine-Guediawaye tribunal.
paragraphs: Three popular TikTok personalities, known as Rox, Jessica, and Narou, have been placed under arrest warrant and will be detained until their trial on Wednesday. The prosecutor, Dicko, requested their pre-trial detention, which was granted by a magistrate. They will be held at the Liberté 6 women's prison.

Rox faces four charges, while Jessica and Narou face fewer, though the specific nature of these offenses has not been detailed. The case will be heard as a flagrant délit, an expedited procedure for offenses observed at the time of their commission. This allows for a swift resolution of the matter.

The women, identified as Rokhaya Fall, Khadidiatou Kébé, and Nafi Fall, are accused of public indecency and offenses against good morals. Despite attempts to withdraw their complaints following their arrest by the cybersecurity division, the prosecutor's decision to detain them remains unchanged.

sn.headline: Sculptor Carves River Mystery into Historic Tree
sn.dek: Lamine Sarr, 71, is completing "Kemaan gui," a monumental sculpture on the Podor quay, started in 1997 and resumed in 2023.
paragraphs: At 71, Senegalese sculptor Lamine Sarr is dedicating his time to completing "Kemaan gui" (the mystery), a monumental sculpture carved into a historic caïlcédrat tree on the Quai de Podor. The municipality granted him the tree in 1997, the same year he began the work, which depicts a siren, arms like hair, the river, a canoe, and a harpooner. After a pause of over two decades, Sarr resumed carving in December 2023, driven by a desire to create a lasting landmark.

Sarr, who returned to Senegal in 1989 after years in Mauritania, views his work as a testament to his connection to the region, drawing inspiration from the river, its boats, and its people. He compares his ambition for longevity to that of creators of iconic structures like the Statue of Liberty and the Eiffel Tower. The sculpture, which uses the tree as its material, monument, and memory, aims to endure through generations.

His deep connection to the river stems from his upbringing in Podor and his family ties across the border in Mauritania, where his mother was from. Sarr considers the river a natural boundary that divides, yet unites, the same people, with families often split by its flow. This personal history informs his artistic vision for "Kemaan gui."

sl.headline: Charcoal burning deforests Sierra Leone, threatens food security
sl.dek: Environmental officials acknowledge limited alternatives as the practice of burning wood for charcoal accelerates deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions.
paragraphs: Charcoal burning, a common practice across Sierra Leone, is leading to significant deforestation and environmental degradation, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. The process, which involves cutting down trees, including valuable fruit-bearing ones like mango and orange, emits greenhouse gases and contributes to habitat loss. Director of Natural Resource Governance, Paul Lamin, stated that the practice leaves land treeless and vulnerable to climate change, while also threatening food security.

The demand for charcoal is high, especially in Freetown and other regional towns, because only 36% of the population has access to electricity and a mere 15% have access to clean cooking. This lack of alternative energy sources forces many households, particularly those with lower incomes, to rely on charcoal despite its environmental impact. Experts warn that the burning of wood for charcoal and its subsequent use as fuel releases substantial greenhouse gases, harming both human health and the environment.

The Food and Agricultural Organization estimates that traditional wood energy, including charcoal, emits 2.4 GT of carbon dioxide equivalent annually, representing 2-7% of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions. The agency warns that continued unsustainable charcoal production and use, driven by increasing demand, will exacerbate climate change. This, in turn, could negatively impact forests and woodlands, reducing future wood-energy supplies.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone Vice Presidents Face Political Dead End
sl.dek: The constitution grants significant power to the vice presidency, but historical precedent shows it rarely leads to the top office.
paragraphs: The office of Vice President in Sierra Leone, constitutionally second only to the president, has historically served as a political cul-de-sac rather than a pathway to leadership. Analysis suggests that vice presidents are often appointed to balance regional, religious, or ethnic considerations, appease party factions, neutralize rivals, or reward loyalty, rather than to cultivate future presidential ambitions. This practice frequently leaves vice presidents without a clear succession plan or an independent political base upon entering office.

Post-independence history provides numerous examples of this trend. Vice presidents like Sorie Ibrahim Koroma and Francis Minah were powerful figures but not groomed for succession, with Minah's case illustrating the dangers of proximity to power without political insulation. Solomon Ekuma Berewa, despite being well-prepared and involved in governance, lost the 2007 presidential election, demonstrating that competence in the vice presidential role does not guarantee electoral success.

More recent examples, such as Victor Bockarie Foh's brief and politically constrained tenure, and Samuel Sam-Sumana's experience of being estranged, expelled, and politically orphaned after his election, further underscore the precarious nature of the vice presidency. These instances collectively suggest that the office, while constitutionally significant, often fails to provide political security or a viable route to the presidency for its occupants.

sl.headline: Women Face Rape and Harassment in Sierra Leone Mines
sl.dek: Artisanal miners in Kono district recount sexual violence and exploitation as they seek income from abandoned sites.
paragraphs: Women in Sierra Leone's Kono district are facing severe sexual violence, including rape and harassment, while working in abandoned mining sites. Janet, 32, shared her experience of being raped at 15 while scavenging for diamonds and gold in Jaiama Nimikor. She became pregnant and later stigmatized, with a relative raising her child. For many women, including widows like Haja, 48, mining became a primary source of income after the civil war and the death of their husbands, forcing them into dangerous environments.

Haja fled her community after being raped by a man in the village, leaving her children behind due to shame. She reported the incident, but the camp master dismissed her claim, suggesting the perpetrator was her boyfriend. Haja eventually returned after her daughter's plea. These accounts highlight the pervasive dangers and lack of recourse for women in artisanal mining, where they often work alone or in precarious conditions.

The pursuit of income from abandoned mines in the diamond-rich Kono district, a consequence of the civil war, has exposed women to exploitation. Many, like Janet, dropped out of school due to poverty and relied on scavenging in old pits. The trauma of sexual assault and its aftermath, including unwanted pregnancies and community stigma, has had a lasting impact on their lives and livelihoods.

sl.headline: SLEWRC revenue jumps to NLE 7.4 million
sl.dek: The Sierra Leone Electricity and Water Regulatory Commission increased internal revenue from NLE 2.3 million in 2023 to NLE 7.4 million in 2024 through levies and licenses.
paragraphs: The Sierra Leone Electricity and Water Regulatory Commission (SLEWRC) reported a significant increase in its internal revenue generation, reaching NLE 7.4 million in 2024. This figure represents a substantial rise from the NLE 2.3 million collected in 2023, primarily from levies and licenses. Despite not receiving budgeted funds from the Ministry of Finance for operational expenditures in both 2023 and 2024, the commission successfully completed key deliverables.

so.headline: Laftagaren forces attack Baidoa, seize army bases
so.dek: Fierce gun battles erupted in Baidoa after forces loyal to ousted leader Abdiasis Laftagaren attacked from multiple directions, seizing two federal army bases.
paragraphs: Heavy fighting broke out in Baidoa on Thursday when forces loyal to former Southwest State President Abdiasis Laftagaren attacked the city from several directions. The attackers seized two federal army bases on the city's outskirts before entering Baidoa and engaging government troops in hours of intense gun battles. A spokesman for Laftagaren's Darwish forces stated they would continue fighting until the last federal soldier departed the region and control was fully restored to the people. The forces later withdrew from the city, ending the confrontation.

Southwest State Information Minister Nur Sidow claimed in Baidoa that Al-Shabaab was responsible for the attack, initiating it with suicide car bombs. The Somali federal government made a similar assertion last month following a prior attack by Laftagaren's forces on Baidoa. However, regional authorities and the federal government have not yet presented any concrete evidence to support the claim that Al-Shabaab was involved.

The recent clashes resulted in multiple fatalities and other casualties, though official figures remain unavailable. Among those killed was the commander of the personal guards for the current Southwest leader, Adan Madobe. Isaq Abdulle, commander of the Somali army’s 8th Brigade of the 60th Division, suffered serious injuries. Analysts note that Baidoa, once peaceful under Laftagaren, has become a battleground since his removal, with recurrent fighting challenging federal control.

so.headline: Somalia Holds First Regional Anti-FGM Hearing
so.dek: East African Legislative Assembly members met with Somali officials and civil society in Mogadishu to discuss a bill aimed at combating female genital mutilation.
paragraphs: Mogadishu hosted Somalia's inaugural public consultation with the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA) concerning a proposed regional framework to combat female genital mutilation (FGM). Somali government officials, regional lawmakers, religious leaders, and civil society representatives participated in the two-day hearing on the Elimination of Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) Bill, 2025. This event marks Somalia's first in-country engagement with EALA since its integration into the eight-member regional bloc at the end of 2025.

The consultation holds particular significance given Somalia's FGM prevalence, estimated at 99% of women and girls according to the 2020 Somali Demographic and Health Survey. The country currently lacks a specific national law prohibiting the practice. Equality Now, which organized the hybrid hearing, emphasized the importance of gathering opinions and recommendations from Somali stakeholders to foster acceptance of the proposed legislation.

Participants reviewed the bill clause by clause, focusing on strengthening protection mechanisms, enhancing cross-border cooperation, and coordinating regional actions against FGM. EALA member Falhada Dekow Iman, a sponsor of the bill, stated that the legislation should not be perceived as an attack on communities or their traditions. The hearing brought together representatives from federal government institutions, Somali and EALA lawmakers, and various civil society groups.

so.headline: Somalia, Qatar University Sign Technology Education Pact
so.dek: A new university focused on high-quality technical and vocational training will be established with support from the University of Doha for Science and Technology.
paragraphs: Somalia's Ministry of Education, Culture and Higher Education has signed a cooperation agreement with the University of Doha for Science and Technology (UDST) to establish the Technology University (TUS University). The pact, signed in Doha, outlines a framework for developing a university specializing in technical and vocational education.

Under the partnership, UDST will provide support for curriculum development, teacher training, quality assurance, and certification. The initial phase will concentrate on critical fields such as technology, marine sciences, aviation, petroleum, engineering, energy, and health management, aiming to enhance the skills of Somali youth.

This initiative aligns with Somalia’s National Transformation Plan 2025–2029, seeking to improve educational quality and develop labor market-aligned skills. A key focus will be training Somali teachers to staff the new university's administration and academic departments, with appreciation extended to Qatar for its ongoing support.

so.headline: Militias Seize Somali Election Centers Amid Opposition
so.dek: Armed groups occupied voter registration sites in Beledweyne, protesting planned elections and demanding fairness in candidate selection.
paragraphs: Armed militias occupied voter registration centers in Beledweyne on Tuesday, escalating opposition to the September 30 Hirshabelle municipal and parliamentary elections. The militias stated their objection to elections managed by a government-appointed commission, citing a process that allegedly bans all but one favored candidate. The Somali federal government has not yet responded to the militia actions.

Hawadle clan politicians also voiced strong opposition to the planned Hirshabelle election, deeming the process unfair and demanding their turn at the regional administration's presidency. These competing objections have created significant political tension in Beledweyne, directly impacting the designated electoral locations and disrupting the planned voting process.

The dispute centers on claims of a rigged electoral process favoring a single candidate while excluding others, alongside the Hawadle clan's push for leadership. With the electoral commission's date set, the conflict over the fairness and inclusivity of the Hirshabelle elections remains unresolved, and the federal government's stance is pending.

so.headline: Somalia Concludes Security Governance Conference
so.dek: A two-day meeting in Mogadishu focused on strengthening oversight, coordination, and reform across the nation's internal security sector.
paragraphs: Somalia's Ministry of Internal Security has concluded a national conference aimed at enhancing governance and coordination within the country's internal security sector. The two-day event, held September 1-2 in Mogadishu, brought together delegates to discuss strengthening oversight, deepening inter-agency collaboration, and building a financially sustainable security apparatus.

The conference addressed key areas including the Ministry's oversight role over the Somali Police Force, the National Intelligence and Security Agency, and the Immigration and Citizenship Agency. Discussions also covered reporting lines, accountability, performance monitoring, and the balance between operational autonomy and ministerial oversight, alongside federal and member state coordination.

Participants engaged in technical sessions focused on improving coordination gaps between the ministry, its agencies, and the broader security architecture. The agenda also included mechanisms for cooperation, deconfliction of mandates, and information sharing to foster a more cohesive and effective internal security framework.

ss.headline: Professor Duany: South Sudan Fails to Build State Institutions
ss.dek: Weak public administration hinders governance and service delivery, according to the Civil Service Commission chairperson.
paragraphs: South Sudan has not yet built functioning state institutions, declared Prof. Julia Aker Duany, chairperson of the Civil Service Commission. Speaking in Juba, she questioned the nation's progress since independence, stating that institutions remain too weak to address political, economic, and social challenges. Duany argued that the country carried the "tools and mindset of liberation" into state-building, which requires different approaches like stability, effective laws, and responsible resource management.

The inadequacy of public administration is evident, with some institutions lacking basic facilities, including the Civil Service Commission itself, which reportedly has no office. Prof. Duany highlighted the government's struggle to provide essential services such as education, health, and clean water, attributing the failure not to a lack of laws but to institutional inability to implement them. She called for a return to basics and a focus on building institutions capable of enforcing existing legislation.

Despite the criticisms, Duany noted South Sudan's considerable human resources, including many educated citizens, questioning why their potential is underutilized. She suggested learning from other countries while adapting experiences to local contexts and emphasized the need for active citizen participation in strengthening institutions, urging cooperation between government and civil society.

In a related development, the Ministry of Cooperatives and Rural Development received a Toyota Hilux four-wheel-drive vehicle from the Government of Turkey. This donation aims to bolster the ministry's operational capacity and support its field activities, particularly in engaging with rural communities and assisting cocoa and coffee farmers.

Governor Emmanuel Adil Anthony urged officials and citizens to maintain peace during the election period and protect government property. A security report indicated a calm and stable situation in the state over the past three months, with isolated incidents being contained through coordinated efforts by security organs.

ss.headline: Kiir Orders Action on State Broadcaster Challenges
ss.dek: President Salva Kiir has directed urgent solutions for the South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation amid a leadership dispute and ahead of general elections.
paragraphs: President Salva Kiir has ordered an immediate resolution to the operational challenges facing the South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation (SSBC). The directive was issued during a meeting with the Minister of Information, Ateny Wek Ateny, at the State House. The President stressed the broadcaster's critical role in informing the public, especially with the upcoming December general elections.

The meeting followed reports of the SSBC managing director, John Madol Panther, being suspended by the board of directors. Panther, however, dismissed these reports, asserting his continued authority and questioning the board's power to remove him. The Office of the President stated that Ateny presented a progress report on the broadcaster's operational issues.

Kiir emphasized the strategic importance of SSBC and called for coordinated efforts to enhance its capacity, professionalism, and effectiveness. He instructed relevant institutions to collaborate on resolving the identified challenges, ensuring the broadcaster is well-equipped to fulfill its mandate of informing, educating, and entertaining the citizens of South Sudan.

ss.headline: Refugees Return to South Sudan, Embrace Farming
ss.dek: More than 6,000 South Sudanese refugees have returned from Uganda and the DRC and are now cultivating land to rebuild their lives.
paragraphs: Over 6,000 South Sudanese refugees have registered their return to Yei River County since January, according to the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission. The returnees, who came from refugee camps in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo, are now integrating into communities and engaging in farming and other activities. Women and children constitute 70 percent of the arrivals, with men making up the remaining 30 percent.

The returnees cited difficult conditions in refugee camps, including restrictions on accessing land, water, and firewood, as well as hostility from some host communities. Many expressed relief at being back in South Sudan, where they feel safer and have the freedom to cultivate land to feed their families. Despite finding some of their homes and structures destroyed upon arrival, they are focused on rebuilding their livelihoods.

The Relief and Rehabilitation Commission is appealing for increased support from humanitarian partners and well-wishers. Assistance is needed for hospitals, schools, and farms to create a conducive environment for the returnees and to encourage others still in refugee camps to come home. Some returnees are already renting land for cultivation and are determined not to return to the camps.

sd.headline: Sudanese Forces Reject AU Dialogue Initiative
sd.dek: Anti-war groups warned that backing El Burhan's plan could legitimize military rule and deepen Sudan's division.
paragraphs: Sudanese anti-war political and civil forces have rejected the African Union’s endorsement of a proposed “Sudanese-Sudanese Dialogue Initiative.” They submitted a memorandum on September 2 to the AU, warning that the process could legitimize military rule and deepen Sudan’s division. The groups criticized the AU for backing an initiative proposed by Sovereignty Council President Lt Gen Abdelfattah El Burhan, whose October 2021 military coup resulted in Sudan’s suspension from AU activities.

The memorandum stressed that while dialogue is not the problem, any credible political process must be genuinely Sudanese-owned, with participants, agenda, and timing agreed by Sudanese stakeholders. They called for the humanitarian crisis and cessation of hostilities to remain central. The groups also demanded the exclusion of the National Congress Party, the Islamic Movement, and affiliated forces, accusing them of playing a role in starting and prolonging the war. They warned that dialogue without a prior ceasefire or broad participation could entrench fragmentation.

The AU Commission stated its support was based on the need for an inclusive process involving Sudanese civil, political, and societal actors, aiming for a united Sudan governed by legitimate civilian institutions. However, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces aligned-government, Sudan Founding Alliance (Tasees), also rejected the AU endorsement, describing it as biased support for the army's position.

sd.headline: Cholera Outbreak Kills 10 in Sudan's West Kordofan
sd.dek: The World Health Organization has flagged West Kordofan as the latest cholera hotspot after 10 deaths and over 40 infections were recorded in El Idai locality.
paragraphs: At least ten people have died and over 40 have been infected with cholera in Sudan’s West Kordofan region, according to the Kordofan Human Rights Observatory. The cases were reported in El Idai locality over Sunday and Monday. The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified West Kordofan as the latest outbreak hotspot, with more than 2,600 cholera cases reported across several Sudanese states up to early August.

Mortada Ahmed, a spokesperson for the Kordofan Human Rights Observatory, stated that the outbreak is spreading widely in El Idai, with numbers expected to rise. He highlighted a severe lack of medicines and life-saving supplies, including intravenous fluids, and noted that ongoing fighting between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created access difficulties for medical aid and food. Environmental factors from the rainy season, such as stagnant water and increased insect populations, are also contributing to the spread.

The observatory is calling for urgent humanitarian intervention and pressure on warring parties to open safe corridors for essential supplies. The WHO is conducting vaccination campaigns for 928,000 people in West Darfur and West Kordofan, with preventive measures also underway in South and North Darfur. The UN and its partners are intensifying efforts to combat cholera through treatment, vaccinations, and distribution of medical supplies.

At least ten people have died and over 40 have been infected with cholera in Sudan’s West Kordofan region, according to the Kordofan Human Rights Observatory. The cases were reported in El Idai locality over Sunday and Monday. The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified West Kordofan as the latest outbreak hotspot, with more than 2,600 cholera cases reported across several Sudanese states up to early August.

Mortada Ahmed, a spokesperson for the Kordofan Human Rights Observatory, stated that the outbreak is spreading widely in El Idai, with numbers expected to rise. He highlighted a severe lack of medicines and life-saving supplies, including intravenous fluids, and noted that ongoing fighting between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created access difficulties for medical aid and food. Environmental factors from the rainy season, such as stagnant water and increased insect populations, are also contributing to the spread.

The observatory is calling for urgent humanitarian intervention and pressure on warring parties to open safe corridors for essential supplies. sd.headline: WFP Food Aid Destroyed in South Kordofan Air Attack
sd.dek: An airstrike outside Deleng destroyed over 50 metric tons of food aid destined for thousands facing severe food insecurity.
paragraphs: The World Food Programme (WFP) condemned an aerial attack on two of its food aid trucks outside Deleng in South Kordofan on August 30, 2026. The strike destroyed more than 50 metric tons of food, enough to support 5,800 people for a month. The trucks were en route to Kadugli, the state capital, where WFP supports approximately 58,000 individuals experiencing acute food insecurity.

Local authorities reported over 9,800 people arriving in Al-Abbasiya locality, South Kordofan, fleeing renewed fighting. Food and essential household items are among their most urgent needs. Similarly, over 8,700 families from 45 villages have arrived in Shikkan locality, North Kordofan, after fleeing conflict zones. These ongoing displacements strain already overcrowded sites and basic services.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reiterated calls for all parties to protect civilians, humanitarian workers, and supplies, and to ensure rapid, safe, and unhindered access for humanitarian assistance. The Sudan Founding Alliance condemned the attack, calling it a blatant disregard for civilian lives and humanitarian principles.

sd.dek: The Juba City Legislative Council passed a 73.48 billion South Sudanese Pound budget to fund administration and service delivery for the upcoming fiscal year.

She emphasized that the budget provides clarity, stability, and direction for implementing the council’s priorities and strengthens their responsibility to Juba’s residents. Keji expects financial committees and departments to manage public resources within the approved allocations.

Juba City Mayor Christopher Serafino Wani expressed optimism that the new budget will enhance the city administration’s ability to improve services. Deputy Mayor Jennifer Yabu assured the public that the budget would be implemented according to approved plans, committing to using allocated resources for their intended purposes amidst increasing demands for better public services.

tg.headline: Ex-Minister Gnakadé Held for Nearly a Year Awaiting Trial
tg.dek: Former Togolese Minister of the Armed Forces Marguerite Gnakadé faces charges of inciting uprising and remains in detention as her trial date is yet to be set.
paragraphs: Essossimna Marguerite Gnakadé, who served as the former Minister of the Armed Forces under Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, has been in detention for nearly a year. She was arrested on September 17, 2025, at her Lomé residence following public statements critical of the government. Four days later, she was formally charged and placed under a detention order.

The Togolese justice system is prosecuting Gnakadé for alleged "incitement to uprising against the authority." Despite the charges and her prolonged detention since September 2025, the date for her trial has not yet been scheduled. Information regarding the specific location and conditions of her confinement has not been detailed.

Gnakadé's arrest and ongoing detention follow a period of public opposition to the current administration. Her case highlights a legal process that has yet to reach a trial phase, leaving her status uncertain for almost twelve months since her initial apprehension.

tg.headline: Police Arrest Suspect in August Motorcycle Theft Attempt
tg.dek: Togolese police apprehended a 20-year-old man in connection with a failed motorcycle robbery in Lankouvi, while two accomplices remain at large.
paragraphs: A 20-year-old man has been arrested by Togolese national police in connection with a motorcycle theft attempt that occurred on August 26 in Lankouvi. The suspect, identified as D. Sodjiné, a mason residing in Ghana, was apprehended on the same day as the incident. Two other individuals involved in the attempted robbery are currently being sought by authorities.

The incident involved three individuals who, armed with a machete, attempted to steal a BAJAJ 125 BM motorcycle from its owner, A. Kodjo, a carpenter. The attempted theft took place around 3:12 AM. The victim was reportedly saved by the timely arrival of a police patrol unit, which caused the assailants to abandon the motorcycle and flee towards Ghana.

During their escape, the suspects dropped a mobile phone, which was recovered by the police. Analysis of the phone led investigators to Sodjiné. The police have stated their commitment to combating crime and have urged the public to remain vigilant and cooperate with security forces by reporting suspicious activities.

tg.headline: Guin People Celebrate 363rd Kpesoso Ritual
tg.dek: The annual Kpesoso ritual in Glidji marks the sacred stone-taking ceremony and the Guin New Year, fostering unity among diverse clans.
paragraphs: The Guin people of Glidji, Togo, marked the 363rd anniversary of the Kpesoso ritual on Thursday, September 3, 2026. This sacred ceremony, involving the taking of the Sacred Stone, is a central event in the historical capital of Guinyigban. While historians note a discrepancy between the mythical date of 1663 and the historical date of 1680 for the migration of the Gan people, the ritual's importance in Guin religion remains paramount.

The Kpesoso ritual, unique to the Guin in Togo and absent among the Gan in Ghana, is believed to have originated from the traumatic split of the Gan people following a war with the Akwamu. This division led to the formation of the modern Guin people, comprising various clans including Fanti, Anlo, and Afro-Brazilians, united under new leadership and foundational myths.

The ritual, culminating in an oracle that foretells the new year's events, serves as a political and religious tool for social cohesion. It brings together the population and the Vodou priests of 41 official deities, reinforcing national unity and potentially consolidating power against external threats. The following Sunday, the Guin New Year is celebrated with the sharing of 'yekê yekê', a national couscous dish, symbolizing reconciliation and abundance.

tg.headline: French filmmakers leave Togo after provisional release
tg.dek: Two French documentary filmmakers, arrested in July for alleged false declarations, have been permitted to depart Togo.
paragraphs: French filmmakers Gaël Mocaër and Sebastian Perez Pezzani, who were detained in Togo since July 27 while filming a documentary for France Télévisions, have left the country. They were granted provisional liberty and an authorization to exit Togolese territory. A diplomatic source reported that the filmmakers were expected to arrive back in France on Thursday morning.

The French Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed on September 1 that the decision for provisional release was communicated, expressing relief for the families and the ministry's engagement in the matter. The filmmakers, along with their Togolese collaborator Fred Vedomey, were initially arrested in northern Togo. They were subsequently held in Lomé on charges of making false declarations, which they deny, according to their lawyer.

Togolese authorities cited several procedural irregularities, including a lack of necessary permits and the unauthorized use of a drone in a sensitive northern region. This area has experienced jihadist incursions since 2021. Sebastian Perez Pezzani, who had been ill, was previously released in late August for medical treatment, with his passport confiscated at the time.

tg.headline: Opposition Parties Announce Public Conference on Sociopolitical Situation
tg.dek: The National Framework for Consultation for Change will hold a public conference on September 4 in Lomé to discuss the nation's sociopolitical landscape.
paragraphs: Several opposition parties under the National Framework for Consultation for Change (CNCC) are organizing a public conference on September 4 in Lomé. The meeting, initiated by the National Alliance for Change (ANC), Alliance of Democrats for Integral Development (ADDI), Democratic Forces for the Republic (FDR), and the Socialist Pact for Renewal (PSR), aims to address the country's sociopolitical situation. The Ministry of Territorial Administration, Local Governance and Customary Affairs was notified of the event via a letter submitted on August 31, 2026.

The conference is scheduled to take place at 8:30 AM in the MUGET conference hall in Djidjolé. This gathering follows a recent formalization of synergy between the two main opposition blocs, marked by a joint memorandum on August 25 proposing a way out of the political crisis. The momentum was also boosted by a ruling from the ECOWAS Court of Justice, which rejected the constitutional revision adopted in 2024.

Participants in the CNCC conference intend to use the platform to share their perspectives on current events and to continue mobilizing support around institutional issues that have divided Togolese politicians for months. The opposition parties aim to present their analysis of the political climate and foster broader discussion on these divisive matters.

tn.headline: Algeria Converts Desert Barracks into High-Security Prison for Drug Barons
tn.dek: The High Security Council has decided to transform a military barracks in the remote Tanezrouft desert into a high-security facility for drug traffickers.
paragraphs: Algeria is intensifying its response to drug trafficking with a decision to convert a military barracks in the Tanezrouft desert into a high-security prison. The High Security Council, led by President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, made the announcement on Wednesday as part of a broader national strategy to combat drug and psychotropic trafficking. This move aims to strengthen coordination and capabilities against major trafficking networks.

The chosen location, Tanezrouft, is an isolated and inhospitable region in southwestern Algeria, near the Malian border, known for extreme temperatures and vast arid landscapes. The facility will be established within an existing military structure, not a new construction. Details regarding the prison's capacity, operational start date, and the specific categories of inmates have not yet been disclosed by the presidency.

In addition to the new prison, Algeria will establish a specialized security agency focused on combating drug trafficking, modeled after international bodies like the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. This dual approach signifies the government's commitment to a more targeted and robust strategy against significant drug trafficking organizations operating within and through the country.

tn.headline: EU Funds Aid for Tunisian Fire Victims
tn.dek: The European Union has released two hundred thousand euros to support communities impacted by severe fires.
paragraphs: The European Union has allocated two hundred thousand euros in emergency humanitarian funding for Tunisian communities affected by severe fires that began in early June. This financial aid will bolster the efforts of the Tunisian Red Crescent, supported by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, to address a crisis exacerbated by high temperatures, dry vegetation, and strong winds. The funding is intended to provide essential relief and support to those most vulnerable.

According to the Tunisian Red Crescent, fires have already destroyed approximately twelve thousand hectares of forests and agricultural land this season, impacting nearly forty-one thousand four hundred seventy-nine people. These figures include individuals directly affected by the flames and those experiencing disruptions to electricity and water supplies. The fires have damaged or destroyed homes, businesses, farmlands, and fruit trees, severely affecting rural and forest communities reliant on agriculture and natural resources.

The European Union delegation in Tunis stated the funding will facilitate the provision of shelter, essential household items, food aid, financial assistance, and psychosocial support. Activities will also cover water, sanitation, hygiene, and local community engagement. This six-month operation, running until the end of February two thousand twenty-seven, aims to reach fifteen thousand directly affected individuals and is part of the EU's contribution to the IFRC's Disaster Relief Emergency Fund.

tn.headline: Tunisian Court Rejects Appeals in State Security Plot Case
tn.dek: The Court of Cassation upheld convictions for 44 individuals in a case involving accusations of plotting against state security.
paragraphs: Tunis, Tunisia – The Court of Cassation in Tunis has finalized the "conspiracy against state security 1" case by rejecting 46 appeals. On Thursday, September 3, 2026, the court dismissed 44 appeals on their merits and two on procedural grounds, according to judicial sources cited by TAP. This decision concludes a multi-year legal process that has seen significant political figures, businessmen, lawyers, and media personalities facing charges.

The case, which began in February 2023, involved accusations of conspiracy against internal and external state security, forming and joining a terrorist group, and inciting disorder and violence. Some charges also related to undermining food security and the environment. In a previous appeal ruling on November 28, 2025, the Tunis Court of Appeal had issued sentences ranging from five to 45 years imprisonment for those convicted.

Notable figures among those facing charges included Ahmed Néjib Chebbi, Chayma Issa, and Jaouhar Ben Mbarek, with sentences varying significantly from initial rulings. For instance, Kamel Letaïef's sentence was reduced from 66 to 45 years, while Khayam Turki's was reduced from 48 to 35 years. Noureddine Bhiri saw his sentence reduced from 43 to 20 years.

tn.headline: Tunisia Phosphate Uranium Powers Nuclear Energy Plan
tn.dek: Tunisia considers using uranium from its phosphate reserves to build a national nuclear power plant amid a structural energy deficit.
paragraphs: Tunisia faces a severe structural energy deficit, leading to social and economic disruptions like frequent power outages, increased industrial costs, and reduced purchasing power. This crisis is exacerbated by climate change impacts on water resources and consumption peaks, volatile global hydrocarbon markets affecting public finances, and slow progress in renewable energy transitions that are unlikely to meet current demand.

In response to this urgent situation, the idea of utilizing uranium found in Tunisian phosphates to fuel a national nuclear power plant is being presented not as a temporary fix, but as a historic opportunity for strategic change. The country possesses sufficient phosphate reserves containing uranium, which could provide a stable, controllable, and local energy source, potentially driving long-term energy, water, industrial, and geopolitical sovereignty.

Recent European experiences highlight the risks of poor long-term energy planning, with regrets over nuclear phase-outs and renewable energy delays contributing to unprecedented energy cost increases. Germany's economic struggles, marked by industrial bankruptcies, are linked to questionable energy choices and dependence on Russian gas. Tunisia is questioning whether to follow such failed models or secure its future with a stable, local energy source instead of relying on volatile global imports.

Germany's economic struggles, marked by industrial bankruptcies, are linked to questionable energy choices and dependence on Russian gas. Tunisia is questioning whether to follow such failed models or secure its future with a stable, local energy source instead of relying on volatile global imports.

tn.headline: Tunisia Adjusts Poultry Production After Heatwave Losses
tn.dek: The Ministry of Agriculture will assess damages from July and August heatwaves, which caused poultry mortality, slow growth, and reduced productivity.
paragraphs: Tunisia's agriculture ministry is preparing to adjust poultry production following significant losses incurred during an exceptional heatwave in July and August. The extreme temperatures led to poultry mortality, stunted growth, and decreased productivity, particularly affecting broiler farms. This situation was exacerbated by summer electricity and water supply disruptions, which hampered essential ventilation and cooling systems in many small and medium-sized farms.

Salwa Dhaouadi, from the Directorate General of Agricultural Production, stated that the ministry will collaborate with sector stakeholders to precisely evaluate the recorded losses. This assessment aims to determine necessary measures for production adjustments. While some slaughterhouses also experienced disruptions, professionals indicate that the current monthly production drop does not yet constitute a widespread supply crisis, according to the National Chamber of Poultry and White Meat Merchants.

Beyond immediate loss assessment, the ministry plans to learn from this climatic event by adapting farms to climate change and enhancing their resilience to power interruptions. Investing in renewable energy sources for farms is being considered as a key strategy to ensure the continuous operation of critical equipment like ventilation and cooling systems, vital for maintaining suitable conditions for poultry.

zm.headline: Zambia Invests in Cancer Treatment Infrastructure and Decentralization
zm.dek: The Ministry of Health is strengthening oncology services through new equipment, technology, and regional treatment centers.
paragraphs: Zambia has reaffirmed its commitment to enhancing cancer treatment and oncology services across the region. Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary Kennedy Lishimpi stated that this commitment is evident in the nation's investments in specialized cancer treatment infrastructure, equipment, and technology. These efforts were highlighted during the opening of a two-day oncology symposium in Lusaka.

Recent advancements include the commissioning of an upgraded radiotherapy and imaging section by President Hakainde Hichilema, featuring modern technology. The government is also actively decentralizing cancer services. The Ndola Cancer Treatment Centre is nearing 85 percent completion, and a similar facility is planned for Livingstone. These initiatives aim to create a coordinated cancer-care system.

Dr. Lishimpi called for increased collaboration among oncology experts and partners to elevate the quality and safety of cancer treatment. The objective is to ensure patients can access appropriate services closer to their communities, with specialized centers handling advanced and complex cases. This approach seeks to establish a more robust and accessible cancer care network.

zm.headline: Heads of State Inauguration Highlights Zambia's Infrastructure Opportunities
zm.dek: The presence of five African leaders at President Hichilema's inauguration spotlights billions in infrastructure and trade opportunities linked to Zambia's location.
paragraphs: Zambia's geographical position is drawing attention to significant infrastructure, energy, trade, and investment opportunities, according to Ministry of Information and Media Director Spokesperson Henry Kapata. The attendance of leaders from Kenya, Tanzania, Zimbabwe, Namibia, and Botswana at President Hakainde Hichilema’s inauguration on September 1 has highlighted the nation's growing network of potential economic links.

Kapata noted that these neighboring countries are part of an increasingly connected economic network, with railways, highways, border posts, and trade corridors physically linking Zambia to markets from the Indian Ocean to the Atlantic. Namibia's President Nandi-Ndaitwah expressed a desire to strengthen infrastructure for smoother trade, emphasizing the Walvis Bay route and Lobito Corridor connection to Atlantic markets.

Further east, Tanzania is central to the revival of the Tanzania-Zambia Railway Authority (TAZARA), with Zambia, Tanzania, and China signing a US$1.4 billion agreement to revitalize the line connecting Zambia's Copperbelt to the Port of Dar es Salaam. China's involvement signifies Zambia's regional infrastructure agenda attracting international partnerships.

zm.headline: Hichilema begins second term amid Zambia's political divisions
zm.dek: Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema faces the challenge of uniting a nation after a contested election and concerns over political freedoms.
paragraphs: Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema was sworn in for his second five-year term on Tuesday, following an election that highlighted deep political divisions within the country. This marks a more complex beginning to his presidency compared to his first term, which had reinforced Zambia's reputation for peaceful power transitions.

The election's outcome has been disputed, with Hichilema's main challenger facing treason charges and opposition supporters questioning the vote's credibility. The closure of courts during the period for election petitions has also drawn controversy, complicating the political landscape as the president begins his new term.

Political analyst Ngobola Cengelo Muyembe stated that reconciliation requires acknowledging the significant portion of the electorate that supported an alternative candidate. He noted that while President Hichilema spoke of unity and reconciliation in his inaugural address, the reality on the ground must reflect these sentiments for the message to be effective.

zm.headline: Zambia Ministry Rejects UN Report on Treason Law and Detainees
zm.dek: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs disputes the UN Special Rapporteur's characterization of treason as a capital offense and the use of terms like "political detainees."
paragraphs: Zambia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation has formally rejected a recent news release from a United Nations Special Rapporteur. The release, issued on September 2, 2026, addressed post-election developments and contained what the Ministry termed a factual error, prejudicial language, and claims outside the Rapporteur's mandate. The Ministry stated that the Special Rapporteur's office and the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights should issue a public correction.

The primary point of contention is the Special Rapporteur's description of treason as a "capital offence" under Zambian law. The Ministry asserts this is false, citing the abolition of the death penalty in December 2022 and subsequent legislative actions, including accession to the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which entered into force for Zambia on March 19, 2025. No offense in Zambia currently carries the death penalty.

Furthermore, the Ministry disputes the use of terms such as "political detainees" and "post-election crackdown," arguing these present contested claims as fact and prejudge ongoing legal matters. The government contrasted this approach with that of the UN Secretary-General's Special Envoy, who was present and facilitated the handover of opposition figures. The Ministry reaffirmed Zambia's commitment to constitutional democracy and the rule of law.

eh.headline: Sánchez Excludes Morocco, Blames Russia and Israel for Ceuta Crisis
eh.dek: Intelligence reports suggest international networks, not Morocco, fueled the Ceuta border crisis, according to Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
paragraphs: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez stated that Moroccan responsibility has been excluded from the Ceuta crisis, with intelligence services identifying Russia, Israel, and far-right international networks as potential contributors to disinformation. This assessment positions Morocco as an essential partner for resolving the situation, a notable shift from previous border issues involving Western Sahara.

During his first interview of the political year on Cadena SER's 'Hoy por Hoy,' Sánchez dedicated significant time to discussing the Ceuta crisis. He referenced reports from the CNI (National Intelligence Centre) and the unexpected scale of the event, while notably omitting Algeria from the discussion despite a recent visit aimed at improving bilateral relations.

The Prime Minister's remarks suggest a reorientation of blame away from regional neighbors towards broader international actors and extremist groups. The exclusion of Morocco and Algeria from direct responsibility for the crisis's escalation indicates a strategic recalibration in Spain's foreign policy approach to regional stability and border management.

eh.headline: Western Sahara Leader Attends African Union Summit Amidst Rights Campaign
eh.dek: Brahim Ghali participated in the Extraordinary Summit of the African Union in Luanda while analyst Taleb Alisalem vowed to continue speaking out despite threats.
paragraphs: Western Sahara's presence was noted at the African Union summit in Luanda, with leader Brahim Ghali attending alongside other heads of state. The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic holds full membership in the AU, a status predating Morocco's return to the organization in 2017. This participation underscores the ongoing institutional role of the Sahrawi cause on the continent, irrespective of diplomatic efforts to diminish its standing within the AU.

Concurrently, Sahrawi analyst Taleb Alisalem responded to a denunciation by Spanish human rights organizations regarding a campaign of threats and harassment against him. The Spanish Pro-Human Rights League and the International Federation for Human Rights-Spain reported that Alisalem has faced direct threats, personal data dissemination, and public targeting. Alisalem stated, "We will not be silenced! We continue," signaling a resolve to maintain public discourse.

The events highlight the dual assertion of the Sahrawi people's presence in both institutional and public spheres. The analysis of the Sahrawi issue extends beyond decolonization to encompass continental debates on peace, security, and political integration. Furthermore, a Spanish publication recalled Spain's historical responsibility, linking the repression under Franco in Western Sahara to Spain's democratic memory.

eh.headline: Saharaui Republic Affirms African Union Membership
eh.dek: The Saharaui Republic's full membership in the African Union is an institutional reality not subject to Moroccan decision.
paragraphs: The Saharaui Republic maintains its status as a full member of the African Union, a position established in 1982 when it was admitted to the Organization for African Unity. Morocco, which had rejected the decision, left the organization two years later. The Saharaui Republic remained a member as the OAU transitioned into the African Union. Morocco rejoined the AU in 2017, entering an organization where the Saharaui Republic was already a fully recognized member state.

Morocco has since engaged in diplomatic efforts to diminish the international recognition of the Saharaui Republic and shift the balance of power within Africa. While Morocco has secured political support and promoted its autonomy proposal, the African Union's Constitutive Act does not provide a legal mechanism for expelling a member state based on another's challenge to its legitimacy. The AU's charter does, however, allow for the suspension of governments that come to power through unconstitutional means and permits states to voluntarily withdraw.

The Saharaui Republic's participation in African Union summits, with its flag displayed alongside other member states and its delegation attending meetings with institutional parity, underscores its established presence. This institutional standing is not a political concession or dependent on Moroccan recognition, but rather a continuing legal condition within the continental body.

ls.headline: Taxi fire kills community leader, sparks safety probe
ls.dek: Malefu Sephula, 45, died from burns sustained in a taxi blaze two weeks prior, prompting calls for an investigation into public transport safety.
paragraphs: Hundreds gathered to mourn Malefu Sephula, 45, who died on August 14, 2026, from burns sustained in a taxi fire two days earlier. The blaze erupted inside the vehicle minutes after Sephula boarded it on her way to work. Two other passengers, including a child, were hospitalized but survived. The incident has raised questions about bystander conduct, with a family member criticizing someone for filming the event instead of assisting.

Community councillor Lekhooa Molibetsane criticized the misuse of social media for popularity and questioned if the taxi was equipped with a fire extinguisher. Minister of Sports Mputi Stephen Mputi, speaking for the government, called Sephula's death a devastating loss and stated the government's responsibility for public transport safety. He called for a formal investigation into the taxi's condition and the circumstances of the fire.

Allegations suggest the taxi owner, who was reportedly driving, added petrol directly to the engine's carburettor before starting the vehicle. These claims could not be independently verified. Sephula's death is the third tragedy involving fire or road accidents to affect her family, who previously survived a near-fatal incident where she was dragged by a truck.

ls.headline: Man sentenced to 20 years for fatal food row
ls.dek: A Leribe man convicted of culpable homicide must pay M30,000 compensation to the victim's family or serve two decades in prison.
paragraphs: Masupha Katse has been sentenced to 20 years in prison or a M15,000 fine for fatally assaulting ’Mane Mothatjaneng during a village celebration in August 2019. Acting High Court Judge ’Manapo Motebele also ordered Katse to pay M30,000 in compensation to the victim’s family. The altercation began over a dispute about serving meat with papa, a staple food, at a community event in Ha Seetsa.

Justice Motebele rejected Katse’s claim of self-defence, finding that he inflicted the fatal injury during a heat of passion following sudden provocation. While none of the prosecution’s five witnesses saw the fatal blow, the Crown presented circumstantial evidence and informal admissions. The post-mortem identified a severe head injury as the cause of death, though Katse’s defence argued he struck the deceased on the chest and that the victim had a history of violence.

The incident occurred on August 3, 2019, when Katse and another man arrived at a celebration where sheep had been slaughtered. After being served mutton, Katse allegedly commented that only dogs ate meat without papa. A dispute over food escalated when Katse reportedly struck a witness’s hand with a stick, leading to Mothatjaneng’s intervention and the fatal assault. Mothatjaneng died the day after the confrontation.

ls.headline: Econet, GEM Institute Plant 500 Fruit Trees at Lesotho Schools
ls.dek: The 2026 ACT 4 Climate Change Fruit-Up School Drive aims to promote practical climate action and environmental education among young Basotho.
paragraphs: Telecommunications company Econet Telecom Lesotho, in partnership with GEM Institute and UNESCO, launched the 2026 ACT 4 Climate Change Fruit-Up School Drive, which will see over 500 fruit trees planted at 14 schools across six districts. The initiative, launched at Qhomane LECSA High School, is part of a five-year collaboration focused on environmental education and climate action for young people. Learners will participate in tree planting and tree care, fostering a hands-on approach to conservation.

Econet's Public Relations Specialist, Retšelisitsoe Nkhahle, stated that the company's commitment extends beyond telecommunications, emphasizing a responsibility to contribute to the communities and the future of Lesotho. The Fruit-Up program aims to move climate change education from theory to practice, creating greener school environments and providing long-term benefits for schools and surrounding communities. Since 2021, Econet and GEM Institute have planted 3,397 fruit trees at 54 schools, involving over 3,000 learners.

GEM Institute, represented by Tšepang Khau, highlighted the program's role in building environmental and entrepreneurial skills since 2021, encouraging Basotho to recognize the potential of indigenous plants for economic opportunities. UNESCO representative Mankopane Nkhono reaffirmed the organization's support for these initiatives, noting their success in engaging youth in environmental awareness and climate action. The Qhomane LECSA High School principal welcomed the program, with the school receiving 50 apple and peach trees.

ls.headline: Mofomobe asks South Africa to question PM over security links
ls.dek: An opposition leader has petitioned South Africa's Madlanga Commission to seek evidence from Prime Minister Sam Matekane regarding alleged connections to a controversial.
paragraphs: Opposition politician Machesetsa Mofomobe has asked South Africa's Madlanga Commission of Inquiry to question Prime Minister Sam Matekane about his alleged links to businessman Vusimuzi “Cat” Matlala. Matlala testified before the commission, stating he was negotiating to provide VIP protection services to the Lesotho Prime Minister through a company registered in the country. The commission, established in July 2025, is investigating criminality and corruption within South Africa's criminal justice system.

Prime Minister Matekane has denied any knowledge of or business dealings with Matlala, stating he has never met the businessman. However, the Prime Minister's office acknowledged that a former member of his private security detail had engaged with Matlala regarding the establishment of a VIP security company in Lesotho. These dealings, the office stated, were conducted in the former aide's private capacity without the Prime Minister's authorization.

Matlala, who faces criminal charges in South Africa, also testified that General Lesetja Senona, a provincial head of the Hawks, had expressed interest in joining his Lesotho venture, though he was ultimately not hired. Matlala's company was involved in a controversial R228 million police healthcare tender in South Africa, which was later canceled due to corruption allegations. He has also been linked to cartels accused of stealing billions from South African hospitals.

ls.headline: ABC leaders fight, party implodes
ls.dek: Party leader Kabi accuses deputy and SG of insubordination amid deepening crisis.
paragraphs: The once-dominant All Basotho Convention (ABC) party is in crisis as its leadership is at war. Party leader Nkaku Kabi issued a circular accusing his deputy, Samonyane Ntsekele, and Secretary General Thebe Mokoatle of deliberately destabilizing the party. This internal conflict follows an incident where Mr. Mokoatle was reportedly attacked by Mr. Kabi’s bodyguards at a National Executive Committee meeting.

Founded in 2006, the ABC previously dominated Lesotho’s political landscape, winning 51 seats in 2017 and leading the governing coalition. The party suffered a significant loss in the October 2022 polls, securing only eight Proportional Representation seats after losing all 51 constituencies. Mr. Kabi took leadership in February 2022, succeeding Tom Thabane, and has been pursuing a revitalization strategy.

In his circular, Mr. Kabi alleged that Messrs. Mokoatle and Ntsekele have repeatedly disobeyed NEC decisions and worked against his leadership. The party has been plagued by deep internal factionalism since its electoral defeat, with this latest dispute further intensifying the ongoing crisis within the ABC.
